```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)

library(AlphaSimR)
```

## Introduction

Before genomic selection, breeding values were predicted from phenotypes
and pedigrees. Pedigree BLUP, also called the animal model
[@henderson1975Best], combines an individual's own records with those of
its relatives, weighting each relative by how closely related it is. It
remains the standard method in many breeding programs, and in a
simulation it is the natural baseline against which genomic selection is
compared.

`AlphaSimR` provides it through `pedBLUP`, which works like the genomic
prediction functions described in `vignette("GenomicSelection")`: fit a
model to a training population, then apply it to any population with
`setEBV`. This article covers recording the pedigree, the relationships
it implies, fitting the model, and what pedigree prediction can and
cannot do.

## Recording the pedigree

`AlphaSimR` keeps a record of every individual's parents only when asked
to. Pedigree tracking is turned on with `setTrackPed`, and it has to be
turned on before the first population is created, because a pedigree
that starts part way through a simulation is missing the relationships
among its first individuals.

```{r}
set.seed(1975)

founderPop = quickHaplo(nInd = 4, nChr = 1, segSites = 10)

SP = SimParam$new(founderPop)
```
```{r include=FALSE}
SP$nThreads = 1L
```
```{r}
SP$setTrackPed(TRUE)

founders = newPop(founderPop, simParam = SP)
```

## Relationships from a pedigree

The relationships a pedigree implies are summarized by the numerator
relationship matrix $A$, whose off-diagonal elements are twice the
kinship between two individuals and whose diagonal is one plus the
individual's inbreeding coefficient for a diploid. `pedigreeA` calculates
it for a population, and `pedigreeInbreeding` the inbreeding coefficients
alone.

The small pedigree below has two full sibs, a half sib of them, a selfed
individual and a doubled haploid, all descended from the four founders.

```{r}
fullSibs = makeCross(founders, crossPlan = matrix(c(1, 2), nrow = 2,
                                                  ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE),
                     simParam = SP)
halfSib = makeCross(founders, crossPlan = matrix(c(1, 3), nrow = 1),
                    simParam = SP)
selfed = self(founders[1], simParam = SP)
dh = makeDH(founders[1], simParam = SP)

everyone = c(founders, fullSibs, halfSib, selfed, dh)
getPed(everyone)
```

The selfed individual (8) and the doubled haploid (9) appear to have
unknown parents. That is because `self` and `makeDH` default to
`keepParents = TRUE`, which labels the new individual's `mother` and
`father` slots with its parent's parents, here the unknown parents of a
founder. The pedigree recorded in the `SimParam` always holds the real
parent, with a column marking doubled haploids, and it is what the
pedigree functions use:

```{r}
SP$pedigree
```

```{r}
round(pedigreeA(everyone, simParam = SP), 3)
pedigreeInbreeding(everyone, simParam = SP)
```

The matrix shows the familiar values. The founders are unrelated and not
inbred. Full sibs have a relationship of 0.5 and each has 0.5 with each
parent. The half sib has 0.25 with each full sib. Selfing an outbred
founder gives an inbreeding coefficient of 0.5. A doubled haploid is
fully inbred, so its diagonal is 2, and because its genome is two copies
of one gamete from its parent, it is related to everyone else exactly as
that parent is.

Founders made by `runMacs` or `quickHaplo` with `inbred = TRUE` are taken
to be fully inbred rather than outbred. For polyploids, inheritance is
taken to be autopolyploid without double reduction, and the diagonal is
$1 + (v - 1)F$ for ploidy $v$. The details are on the help page of
`pedigreeA`.

The calculation uses the method of @colleau2002Indirect, which never
forms the relationship matrix of the whole pedigree, so it stays fast in
long simulations. `pedigreeA` still returns a dense matrix, so its memory
grows with the square of the number of individuals asked for.

## Fitting the model

The model is $y = Xb + Zu + e$, where $b$ holds the fixed effects, $u$
the breeding values with covariance $A\sigma^2_u$, and $e$ the errors.
`pedBLUP` builds the mixed model equations from the inverse of $A$,
which is sparse, and solves them with a sparse Cholesky factorization.
Unless they are given, the variance components are estimated by
restricted maximum likelihood (REML), using the derivative-free approach
of @graser1987Derivative and @meyer1989Restricted.

The example simulates four generations of random mating in 40 full-sib
families of five, and uses every phenotyped individual to train the
model. A fifth generation, made from the fourth, is the set of selection
candidates. `runMacs` founders are used so that the same population can
later be used for genomic prediction.

```{r}
set.seed(2001)

founderPop = runMacs(nInd = 200, nChr = 10, segSites = 200)

SP = SimParam$new(founderPop)
```
```{r include=FALSE}
SP$nThreads = 1L
```
```{r}
SP$setTrackPed(TRUE)
SP$restrSegSites(minQtlPerChr = 50, minSnpPerChr = 100)
SP$addTraitA(nQtlPerChr = 50)
SP$addSnpChip(nSnpPerChr = 100)
SP$setVarE(h2 = 0.3)

generations = vector("list", 5)
generations[[1]] = newPop(founderPop, simParam = SP)
for(i in 2:5){
  generations[[i]] = randCross(generations[[i - 1]], nCrosses = 40,
                               nProgeny = 5, simParam = SP)
}

trainPop = do.call(c, generations[1:4])
candidates = generations[[5]]
nInd(trainPop)
```

```{r}
pedModel = pedBLUP(trainPop, simParam = SP)

pedModel@Vu
pedModel@Ve
```

The estimates can be compared with the variances the simulation was set
up with, an additive genetic variance of 1 and an error variance of
`r round(SP$varE[1], 3)` in the founders:

```{r}
SP$varA
SP$varE
```

## Predicting with setEBV

As with the genomic models, `setEBV` applies the fit to a population.
`value = "bv"` gives estimated breeding values centered on the training
population, or on `targetPop` when one is supplied, and `value = "gv"`
gives the estimated breeding value plus the estimate for the first level
of the fixed effects, which puts the estimate on the scale of the
phenotypes. The two differ only by a constant, so they rank individuals
identically. `"female"` and `"male"` are not available.

```{r}
candidates = setEBV(candidates, pedModel, value = "bv", simParam = SP)

# Accuracy of the candidates' estimated breeding values
cor(ebv(candidates)[, 1], bv(candidates, simParam = SP)[, 1])
```

The candidates were not in the training population, so they have no
records of their own and no records from descendants. Their best linear
unbiased prediction is then the average of their parents' estimates, and
that is what `setEBV` uses for any individual outside the fit. The same
holds for individuals created long after the model was fitted.

### What a pedigree cannot see

A consequence is that full sibs without records get identical estimates,
because they have identical pedigrees:

```{r}
family = paste(candidates@mother, candidates@father)
estimatesPerFamily = tapply(ebv(candidates)[, 1], family,
                            function(x) length(unique(round(x, 10))))
table(estimatesPerFamily)
```

Every family has a single estimate. The pedigree predicts the average of
a family well, but it carries no information about which sib inherited
the better half of each parent's genome, the Mendelian sampling term
that makes up half of the additive variance in an outbred population.
Markers do carry that information, which is a large part of the
advantage of genomic selection. Fitting `RRBLUP` to the same training
population shows the difference:

```{r}
gsModel = RRBLUP(trainPop, simParam = SP)
gsCandidates = setEBV(candidates, gsModel, value = "bv", simParam = SP)

accuracy = function(x){
  cor(ebv(x)[, 1], bv(x, simParam = SP)[, 1])
}

withinFamily = function(x){
  # The correlation within each family, averaged over families
  df = data.frame(ebv = ebv(x)[, 1], bv = bv(x, simParam = SP)[, 1],
                  family = paste(x@mother, x@father))
  mean(sapply(split(df, df$family), function(f){
    if(sd(f$ebv) == 0) return(0)
    cor(f$ebv, f$bv)
  }))
}

round(rbind(
  pedigree = c(overall = accuracy(candidates),
               withinFamily = withinFamily(candidates)),
  markers = c(overall = accuracy(gsCandidates),
              withinFamily = withinFamily(gsCandidates))
), 3)
```

Overall, markers predict the candidates better than the pedigree does.
The difference comes from within families: the pedigree's within-family
accuracy is zero by construction, while markers rank sibs with an
accuracy well above zero. A larger training population generally widens
the gap, because it improves the estimates of the marker effects, while
records on the candidates themselves would let the pedigree separate sibs
too.

## More than one record per individual

An individual that appears in the training population more than once has
its records treated as repeated records of a single breeding value. That
is how several years of records on a long-lived parent are combined:

```{r}
repeated = c(trainPop, setPheno(generations[[4]], simParam = SP))
nInd(repeated)
length(unique(repeated@id))

repeatModel = pedBLUP(repeated, simParam = SP)
```

No permanent environmental effect is fitted, so any non-additive genetic
variance shared by an individual's repeated records is absorbed into the
estimate of the additive genetic variance.

The `fixEff` slot is fitted as a set of fixed effects, exactly as in the
genomic models. Records from different environments or years should be
labeled with their own `fixEff`, as described in
`vignette("GenomicSelection")`:

```{r}
year1 = setPheno(generations[[3]], fixEff = 1L, simParam = SP)
year2 = setPheno(generations[[4]], fixEff = 2L, simParam = SP)
yearModel = pedBLUP(c(year1, year2), simParam = SP)
yearModel@fixEff
```

## Fitting more cheaply

Estimating the variance components is most of the cost of a fit. Within
one simulation they change slowly, so a common pattern is to estimate
them once and pass that fit as `varComp` in later fits, which then only
solve the mixed model equations. `Vu` and `Ve` can also be given
directly.

```{r}
refit = pedBLUP(trainPop, varComp = pedModel, simParam = SP)

c(refit@Vu, refit@Ve)
```

## Things to know

**The REML search is local.** The variance ratio is searched over two
orders of magnitude either side of the ratio set for the trait in the
`SimParam`, or of 1 when that is not available, first on a grid and then
near its best point. The result is the best ratio found, not a
guaranteed global maximum, and a warning is given if it falls at the
edge of the range. Breeding values change little with the ratio near its
best value.

**No reliabilities are reported.** The output holds estimates, not their
prediction error variances, as with the genomic models.

**A fit belongs to its pedigree.** `resetPed` discards individuals from
the recorded pedigree, and new individuals can then take their internal
IDs. `setEBV` therefore refuses a fit once a reset has discarded any of
the individuals it was fitted to.

**Ploidy changes are not recorded.** A doubled haploid made by
`reduceGenome` followed by `doubleGenome` is recorded as two generations
of selfing, and individuals made by `reduceGenome`, `doubleGenome` or
`mergeGenome` have the wrong relationships. Use `makeDH` for doubled
haploids.

**Only one trait.** `pedBLUP` fits a single trait. A function of several
traits, such as an index, can be passed as `traits` to fit the index as
one trait.
